869.title: The wars of apostasy
869.hook: some tribes refuse zakat or follow new claimants, and Abu Bakr holds the community together
869.howItsDone: Muslims study the riddah as part of early Islamic history, and the exchange between Abu Bakr and Umar about prayer and zakat in Sahih al-Bukhari is often taught in lessons on zakat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr: I am not the best of you. Your line was: set me right. Did you ask anyone to tell you where you could do better? Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

Two friends are arguing, and both of them love the same man who has just died. One is Umar, remembered for his strong words. The other is Abu Bakr, remembered as the gentle one. And in this argument it is the gentle one who will not move. News has reached Medina that tribes across Arabia are pulling away. Some say they will still pray, but they will no longer pay zakat to Medina. Others have gathered around men claiming to be prophets themselves. Umar says: how can we fight people who say there is no god but God? Today's word is the name the sources give this season.
screen: `TWO FRIENDS ARGUE.` → `THE TRIBES PULL AWAY.` → `HOW CAN WE FIGHT THEM?`

segments.voice: Riddah means a turning back. The histories call this time the riddah, and the campaigns of Abu Bakr's rule the wars of the riddah. Bukhari records the argument itself. Umar quotes the Prophet: whoever says there is no god but God has protected his life and his wealth, except by the right of it. Abu Bakr takes hold of those last words. By God, he says, I will fight whoever separates prayer from zakat, because zakat is the right owed on wealth. Even if they hold back a single young goat that they used to give the Messenger of God, I will fight them over it. Then comes the line to hold onto. Umar says: by God, it was nothing but that I saw God had opened Abu Bakr's heart to fight, and I knew it was the truth. The man who started the argument ends it agreeing. So what was being held together? Not only a treasury. The Qur'an itself pairs them: establish the prayer, and give the zakat. To keep one and drop the other was, for Abu Bakr, to start pulling the religion apart at a seam. And the claimants who said they were prophets were pulling at a different seam: the belief that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was the last of the prophets. The histories name some of them, Musaylimah among them. Historians, Muslim and not, have read these campaigns in more than one way: as a defense of the faith, as the holding of a young state together, or both. Sunni and Shia historians also judge some particular episodes differently. What Bukhari keeps for us is quieter: a gentle man refusing to let go, and a stubborn friend who came round.
screen: `RIDDAH: A TURNING BACK.` · `PRAYER AND ZAKAT, NOT ONE WITHOUT THE OTHER.` · `EVEN ONE YOUNG GOAT.` · `UMAR: HIS HEART WAS OPENED.` · then, large: `HOLDING TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep one commitment when it's hard. Let your breath slow. Think of one thing you've promised, to God, to a person, or to yourself, that has started to feel heavy. A daily prayer. A weekly call. A gift you give. Breathe in, and notice the voice that says, just drop this one part and keep the rest. Breathe out. You don't have to argue with it. Just decide, for today only, to keep the whole thing together. One day. The bell holds the time.
Riddah. A turning back: the name the histories give to the tribes' pulling away after the Prophet's death, and to Abu Bakr's campaigns to hold the community together. Today's word.
Your line: holding together. Today, keep one promise whole, even the part you'd rather quietly drop. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

870.title: Abu Bakr's will
870.hook: dying, he names Umar and leaves almost nothing (reported)
870.howItsDone: Muslims retell Abu Bakr's deathbed request for a washed, worn garment as a lesson in simplicity; his grave lies beside the Prophet's in the mosque at Medina.

segments.voice: Yesterday, riddah, the turning back, and a gentle man who would not let prayer and zakat be pulled apart. Your line was: holding together. Which promise did you keep whole? Day eight hundred seventy.

An old man lies ill, and he asks his daughter a strange question. In how many cloths was the Prophet wrapped for burial? Then another: on what day did the Prophet die? Monday, she says. And what day is it today? Monday again. He hopes, he says, to die before tonight is out. The daughter is Aisha. The father is Abu Bakr, the khalifah, leader of the whole community. And the questions he is asking are the questions of a man arranging his own departure as simply as he can. Today: Abu Bakr's will.
screen: `WHAT DAY DID THE PROPHET DIE?` → `HOW MANY CLOTHS?` → `ARRANGING HIS OWN DEPARTURE.`

segments.voice: Bukhari keeps the scene. Aisha's answer to the first question: the Prophet was wrapped in three white cloths. Abu Bakr looks at the garment he has been wearing in his illness, which has a stain of saffron on it. Wash this one, he says, and add two more, and wrap me in them. Aisha protests: but it's worn. And he answers: the living have more right to the new than the dead. It is only for what the body gives back to the earth. The leader of the whole community, asking to be buried in a used garment. The histories add more, and they are clear that these are reports. Tradition says Abu Bakr asked that whatever his household had gained while he held office be handed on to the next leader. When it arrived, the reports describe very little: an animal, a servant, a worn cloth. And they say Umar wept and said, you have made it hard for whoever comes after you. Before he died, the histories also say, Abu Bakr consulted some of the companions and then had it written that Umar would lead after him. Sunni Muslims see this as a rightful choice made by a rightful caliph. Shia Muslims, as earlier days described, see the whole succession differently. The reports themselves describe a man who did not get rich from power. And he was buried in Aisha's room, beside the friend he had followed. So the part of the story that began with the day after, the succession, ends here: a pledge, a speech, a hard season, and a man who left almost nothing. Tomorrow a new part begins, with Umar.
screen: `THREE WHITE CLOTHS.` · `WASH THIS ONE, AND ADD TWO.` · `THE LIVING HAVE MORE RIGHT TO THE NEW.` · `YOU HAVE MADE IT HARD FOR WHOEVER COMES NEXT.` · then, large: `HE LEFT ALMOST NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The practice: plan to leave little behind. Breathe once, slowly, and bring to mind the things you own that you never use. A drawer. A closet. A shelf. Breathe in, and picture the people who would one day have to sort through it. Breathe out. Choose one thing, just one, that someone living needs more than you do: a coat, a tool, a book. Decide where it's going. The living have more right to the new. The bell holds the time.
Abu Bakr's will. A worn garment for his shroud, his gains in office handed back, Umar named after him, and a grave beside the Prophet. Today's word.
Your line: he left almost nothing. Today, give away one thing you don't use to someone who will. Day eight hundred seventy.

871.title: The calendar
871.hook: Umar dates the Muslim calendar from the Hijra
871.howItsDone: Muslims use the Hijri calendar for Ramadan, the two Eids, the Hajj and other religious dates, beginning each month with the new crescent moon, alongside the solar calendar for everyday life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr's will: a washed, worn garment for a shroud, and a successor named. Your line was: he left almost nothing. What did you give away? Day eight hundred seventy-one.

A document reaches Umar, the histories say, dated in the month of Sha'ban. Fine. But which Sha'ban? This year's? Last year's? Letters and records are coming in from far away, and a month name alone can't put them in order, or tell you how old a promise is. A new part of our story begins today, with Umar leading the believers, and it begins with a very practical problem: where do you start counting? Today: the calendar.
screen: `A LETTER: WHICH SHA'BAN?` → `NOBODY CAN TELL THE ORDER.` → `WHERE DO YOU START COUNTING?`

segments.voice: The months themselves were already there. The Qur'an speaks of them in Pickthall's words: "Lo! the number of the months with Allah is twelve months by Allah's ordinance in the day that He created the heavens and the earth." And elsewhere it says the new moons are markers of time for people and for the pilgrimage. So the months follow the moon: a new month when the new crescent appears. What was missing was a year one. The histories say Umar gathered the companions to decide, and that ideas were offered. You could count from the Prophet's birth. From the first revelation. From his death. Bukhari keeps a short report from the companion Sahl ibn Sa'd that settles what they chose: they did not count from the Prophet's mission, nor from his death, but from his arrival in Medina. The Hijra. The migration. Tradition says it was Ali who suggested it, and Umar who decided it. Look at what they passed over. They didn't choose the moment the message began, or the moment the Prophet was taken from them. They chose the moment a small community left home and found a place to live their faith openly. Year one is a journey. Every date in that calendar since quietly says: counted from the migration. Muslims mark the new Hijri year at the start of the month of Muharram, and in that same month comes Ashura: Shia Muslims keep it in mourning for Husayn, and among Sunni Muslims it is a day of voluntary fasting. The same calendar, carrying different memories.
screen: `THE MONTHS FOLLOW THE MOON.` · `WHAT WAS MISSING WAS A YEAR ONE.` · `NOT THE MISSION, NOT HIS DEATH.` · `FROM HIS ARRIVAL IN MEDINA.` · then, large: `COUNTED FROM THE MIGRATION.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn today's Hijri date. If you have a phone nearby, look it up after the bell: the day, the month and the year. For now, let your breath slow. Think of the moon tonight, wherever it is in its cycle, and of the month it's marking. Breathe in, and think of the migration: a group of people leaving what they knew for a place where they could live what they believed. Breathe out. Ask yourself: where would I start counting my own year one? The bell holds the time.
The calendar. The Hijri calendar: months that follow the moon, and years counted from the Prophet's migration to Medina, a choice the histories credit to Umar. Today's word.
Your line: counted from the migration. Today, learn the Hijri date, and say it once to someone. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

872.title: The register
872.hook: Umar sets up stipends, including for the poor and newborns (reported)
872.howItsDone: Muslims often retell the story of Umar and the crying baby in sermons on justice and care for the vulnerable, and the diwan is taught in Islamic history as an early public register.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the calendar: moon months, and a year one chosen in Umar's time. Your line was: counted from the migration. Did you find today's Hijri date? Day eight hundred seventy-two.

A baby is crying behind a door in Medina, and it will not stop. Not the ordinary crying of a tired baby. This one goes on and on. A man walking the streets in the dark stops at the door and tells the mother to look after her child. Later he passes again, and the baby is still crying. He asks what's wrong. She doesn't know who she's speaking to. She tells him she is weaning the child early, because the stipend is only paid for children once they are weaned. The man walking the streets is Umar. Today's word: the register behind that rule.
screen: `A BABY CRYING IN THE NIGHT.` → `WEANED EARLY, FOR THE STIPEND.` → `THE MAN AT THE DOOR IS UMAR.`

segments.voice: Diwan means a register: a book of names. The histories say Umar set one up in Medina as wealth began to come in, listing the people of the community so that each could receive a regular share, an ata, from the public treasury. The reports describe the Prophet's family, the companions, the fighters and their households, written in by name. It sounds dry: a list. But a list decides who counts. Now back to the crying baby. This part comes from the early histories, not the hadith collections, and is told as a story. When the mother explains, Umar is shaken. Tradition says that at the dawn prayer the people could hardly understand his recitation for his weeping, and that afterward he said something like: woe to Umar, how many children has he harmed? Then he had it announced: do not hurry to wean your children; we will give a share for every child born in Islam. From birth, not from weaning. The Qur'an says mothers may nurse their children for two whole years, for those who want to complete the nursing. A rule written for the treasury had quietly pushed against that, and against a baby's hunger. One crying child, heard by the right person at night, changed the register. And look at what Umar did not say. He didn't blame the mother. He didn't defend the rule because it was his. He looked at who the rule was hurting, and he rewrote it. A register is only as just as the people it remembers to write in.
screen: `DIWAN: A REGISTER OF NAMES.` · `A REGULAR SHARE FROM THE TREASURY.` · `A RULE THAT HURT A BABY.` · `FROM BIRTH, NOT FROM WEANING.` · then, large: `A SHARE FOR EVERY CHILD.`

segments.voice: The practice: support a family with a new baby. Rest your hands, and bring to mind someone you know who has a new baby, or is expecting one, or is raising a little one with very little help. Breathe in, and picture their night: the crying, the tiredness, the counting of money. Breathe out. Choose one small, practical thing you could do for them this week. A meal. An hour of holding the baby. Diapers. A message that says you're thinking of them. If you pray, you can ask for ease for them. The bell holds the time.
Diwan. A register of names: in Umar's time, the list that gave each person in the community a regular share from the treasury, and, the story says, every child from birth. Today's word.
Your line: a share for every child. Today, do one small, practical thing for a family with a little one. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

873.title: Umar at Jerusalem
873.hook: Umar receives Jerusalem's surrender, and tradition says he prayed outside the church so it would stay a church
873.howItsDone: Muslims and Christians in Jerusalem both retell the story of Umar praying outside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and a mosque named for Umar stands nearby.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the diwan, and a crying baby that changed a rule. Your line was: a share for every child. What did you do for a family with a little one? Day eight hundred seventy-three.

It's time to pray, and the leader of the believers is standing inside a church. Not just any church: the great church in Jerusalem that Christians built over the place where they remember Christ's tomb. The city has just surrendered. The patriarch who handed it over is beside him. And Umar, the story goes, is asked to pray right there, inside. He says no. Today: Umar at Jerusalem, and why, as the story is told, he stepped outside.
screen: `TIME TO PRAY, INSIDE A CHURCH.` → `THE CITY HAS SURRENDERED.` → `UMAR SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. The Qur'an and hadith don't tell this story. It comes from later chroniclers, one of them a Christian patriarch of Alexandria, and Muslims and Christians have both retold it. It is tradition, not scripture. Jerusalem's patriarch, Sophronius, agreed to surrender the city, but only to the caliph himself. So Umar came. The histories preserve a covenant of safety for the people of the city, which in its usual form promises them their lives, their property and their churches: the churches would not be lived in, torn down or reduced. The versions of that document differ, and scholars debate its wording. Then the story. While Umar was being shown the Church of the Resurrection, the time of prayer came. The patriarch invited him to pray where he stood. Umar declined. If I pray here, he is reported to have said, the Muslims after me will take it, saying: Umar prayed here. So he went out and prayed on the steps outside, alone. Tradition places a mosque named for him near that spot, and the church still stands as a church. Look at the shape of it. The man with every power to take the building chose a smaller thing: to protect it from his own followers' devotion to him. He knew his prayer would become a claim. So he prayed outside. The Qur'an itself names cloisters, churches, synagogues and mosques together as places where God's name is remembered much, places it says would have been pulled down if God did not check one people by another.
screen: `A STORY FROM LATER CHRONICLERS.` · `A COVENANT FOR THE CHURCHES.` · `IF I PRAY HERE, THEY WILL TAKE IT.` · `HE PRAYED ON THE STEPS OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `HE PRAYED OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: The practice: respect another's holy place. Let a long breath out, and bring to mind a place that's holy to someone else: a church, a temple, a synagogue, a gurdwara, a grave, a corner of a friend's home where they pray. Breathe in, and picture yourself at its door. Breathe out. Ask what it would mean to honor it on its own terms: to take off your shoes, or lower your voice, or simply not take a photo. If you pass such a place today, give it that respect. The bell holds the time.
Al-Quds, the holy, Jerusalem's Arabic name: the city where Umar, the caliph, received its surrender and stepped outside a church to pray so it would stay a church. Today's word.
Your line: he prayed outside. Today, when you enter someone else's space, holy or ordinary, leave it as you found it. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

874.title: Justice for a Coptic boy
874.hook: a well-known report tells how Umar punished a governor's son for striking an Egyptian: since when have you enslaved people born free
874.howItsDone: Muslims often quote Umar's line 'since when have you enslaved people when their mothers bore them free?' in sermons and writing on justice and human dignity, though the report comes from history, not the hadith collections.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umar at al-Quds, stepping outside so a church would stay a church. Your line was: he prayed outside. Whose space did you leave as you found it? Day eight hundred seventy-four.

A horse race in Egypt. Two young men, two horses, and the wrong one wins. The winner is a Copt, an Egyptian Christian. The loser is the son of the governor, Amr ibn al-As, the man who rules the province for Umar. And the governor's son does what a certain kind of powerful young man does when he loses. He takes a whip to the winner, and as he strikes he says: take that, I am the son of the noble ones. Today: justice for a Coptic boy.
screen: `A HORSE RACE IN EGYPT.` → `THE GOVERNOR'S SON LOSES.` → `I AM THE SON OF THE NOBLE ONES.`

segments.voice: The story comes from a history of the conquest of Egypt, not from the hadith collections. It is a report people tell, not a verified hadith. The Copt doesn't take the beating quietly. He travels all the way to Medina and stands before Umar. Umar listens, and sends for the governor and his son to come too. When they arrive, Umar hands the whip to the Egyptian. Strike, he says, the son of the noble ones. And the Copt does. Then Umar turns to the governor himself, the father, the powerful man whose name had made his son feel untouchable, and says the line the story is remembered for: since when have you enslaved people, when their mothers bore them free? Listen to what that claims. Free from the womb. Not free because of your father's rank, or your tribe, or your faith. Free because you were born. And notice who stands where. A Christian subject of a Muslim state crosses a desert to accuse the son of a Muslim governor, and the caliph hands him the whip. The Qur'an calls for this kind of evenhandedness: it tells believers to stand firm for justice as witnesses for God, even against themselves, or their parents, or their kin, whether rich or poor. The story puts that verse on a dusty road between Egypt and Medina. Whatever happened on that road, the line is why the story lasts. Born free.
screen: `A REPORT, NOT A HADITH.` · `THE COPT CROSSES TO MEDINA.` · `UMAR HANDS HIM THE WHIP.` · `JUSTICE, EVEN AGAINST YOUR KIN.` · then, large: `WHEN THEIR MOTHERS BORE THEM FREE.`

segments.voice: The practice: defend someone's dignity. Sit up a little, breathe, and bring to mind a person who gets treated as smaller than they are. Someone who cleans your office. A new kid at school. A neighbor whose accent people mock. Breathe in, and say to yourself, about them: born free. Breathe out. Now think of one moment this week when you could stand up for them, even quietly. Using their name. Correcting a joke. Thanking them in front of others. Choose it. The bell holds the time.
Copt, an Egyptian Christian: the young man a governor's son struck with a whip, until Umar handed him the whip himself and asked, since when have you enslaved people born free? Today's word.
Your line: born free. Today, treat one person the world overlooks as exactly as free and as worthy as anyone. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

875.title: The plague
875.hook: Umar turns back from a plague region, and a companion quotes the Prophet ﷺ: don't enter or leave a plague land (Bukhari)
875.howItsDone: Muslim scholars cite the Prophet's teaching on plague, and Umar's turning back, when giving guidance on epidemics: avoid entering an affected place, and don't flee from one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice for a Copt, and a whip handed to the one who'd been struck. Your line was: born free. Whose dignity did you stand up for? Day eight hundred seventy-five.

A caravan is halted on the road north. At its head is Umar, on his way to Syria. Riding out to meet him come his commanders, Abu Ubaydah among them, and they bring news nobody wants: plague has broken out in the land ahead. Behind Umar ride companions of the Prophet, emigrants and Ansar. Ahead is a sickness no one can see. Do you go on, trusting God? Or do you turn around? Today: the plague.
screen: `A CARAVAN HALTED ON THE ROAD.` → `PLAGUE IN THE LAND AHEAD.` → `GO ON, OR TURN BACK?`

segments.voice: Bukhari tells it in detail. Umar calls the early emigrants and asks them. They disagree: some say go on, some say turn back. He calls the Ansar of Medina. They disagree too. Then he calls the elders of Quraysh, and they speak with one voice: turn back, don't lead the people into the plague. So Umar announces they will leave in the morning. And Abu Ubaydah, his old friend, objects: are you running from the decree of God? Umar answers with a picture. Yes, he says, we are running from the decree of God to the decree of God. If you had camels and came to a valley with two slopes, one green and one bare, and you grazed them on the green, wouldn't that be by God's decree? And if you grazed them on the bare, wouldn't that be by God's decree too? Choosing the safer slope is not leaving God's will. It is moving within it. Then a companion who had been away arrives: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. And he says: I have knowledge of this. I heard the Messenger of God say, if you hear of it in a land, don't go into it; and if it breaks out in a land where you are, don't leave it to flee from it. Umar praises God, and turns back. Notice the order. Umar consulted, decided, and then found that the Prophet's teaching agreed. Don't enter. Don't leave. Many readers today hear in those two lines what we now call quarantine.
screen: `EMIGRANTS, ANSAR, ELDERS: HE CONSULTS.` · `FROM GOD'S DECREE TO GOD'S DECREE.` · `TWO SLOPES, ONE GREEN, ONE BARE.` · `ABD AL-RAHMAN: I HEARD THE PROPHET.` · then, large: `DON'T ENTER, DON'T LEAVE.`

segments.voice: The practice: follow sound health advice. Breathe in through the nose, out slowly, and bring to mind one piece of good advice about your health that you've been putting off. Seeing a doctor. Staying home when you're sick. Taking a medicine properly. Resting. Breathe in, and hear Umar: we run from God's decree to God's decree. Breathe out. In Umar's picture, taking care is not a lack of trust. The green slope is still God's slope. Decide on one step, and when you'll take it. The bell holds the time.
The plague. The outbreak that turned Umar back on the road to Syria, and the Prophet's teaching, recalled by Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: don't go into a plague land, and don't flee from one. Today's word.

Your line: don't enter, don't leave. Today, take one step to protect your health, or someone else's. And look back at the week: riddah, a will, a calendar, a register, Jerusalem, a Coptic boy, and a caravan turned back. Day eight hundred seventy-five.
screen: `THIS WEEK: RIDDAH · THE WILL · THE CALENDAR · THE DIWAN · JERUSALEM · BORN FREE · THE PLAGUE.`
